item.title: View of Toledo
item.museum: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
item.lesson: Domenikos Theotokopoulos — 'El Greco,' the Greek — trained as a Byzantine icon painter in Crete, absorbed Titian's color in Venice, and settled in Toledo, where his elongated, flame-like style found its home. This is one of only two surviving landscapes he painted, and it is less a view than a vision: he rearranged the city freely, moving the cathedral's spire, so that Toledo could sit under a sky that seems about to split open. Green-black storm light rolls over the hills; the buildings glow an unearthly gray. No one in Europe was painting weather as emotion in 1600 — landscape this subjective would not really return until the Romantics two centuries later, and painters like Cézanne and the German Expressionists claimed El Greco as a direct ancestor. It hung nearly forgotten until the modern age recognized one of its own.
item.lookFor: Notice what is missing: the sun. The entire city is lit by storm light with no visible source, as if illuminated from inside the ground.
